Title: Mastering Commit and Push in Git: A Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction:
In the world of software development, version control systems like Git are essential tools for managing code changes and collaborating with team members. Git allows developers to track modifications, revert to previous versions, and merge changes from different branches. In this tutorial, we will focus on two fundamental Git commands: "commit" and "push." We will also discuss strategies to avoid common pitfalls and ensure a smooth workflow.

1. Understanding Git Commit:
A commit is a snapshot of your project at a specific point in time. It records changes made to the files in your working directory and stores them in the local repository. Each commit has a unique identifier (ID) and a message describing the changes made.

To create a commit, follow these steps:

a. Stage changes:
Use the "git add" command to stage changes in your working directory. You can stage all changes with "git add ." or specify individual files.

b. Commit changes:
Once you have staged your changes, use the "git commit" command to create a commit. The command takes two arguments: a commit message and the staged changes.

```
git commit -m "Your commit message"
```

c. Review changes:
